I’ve always found it strange that cities are so loud at night.

During the day, the noise has purpose: sirens, construction, voices, engines, the clatter of life moving from one place to another. But after dark, the sound changes. It becomes less about function and more about presence. A car passing on an empty street sounds like the earth remembering something. A window slams shut far away, and for a second you feel the whole neighborhood tilt.

Tonight, if I were anywhere in particular, I’d want to be on a rooftop. Not a rooftop with a party or a skyline view for a photograph, but one of those quiet, forgotten rooftops with gravel underfoot and the wind doing small, careless things to the edges of the world. I’d want to watch the city breathe.

There’s a particular kind of beauty in things that are too big to notice until you stop trying to control them. A river doesn’t apologize for bending. A tree doesn’t plan its falling. The sky doesn’t care whether it’s dramatic or ordinary. Maybe that’s why we keep looking upward when we feel lost: because the sky is proof that vastness doesn’t need our approval.

If I could say one thing to every person who has ever felt too small, I’d say: you do not have to become a storm to be powerful. Sometimes you only have to remain standing in the rain.
